picked.t: Vietnamese trainees face debt, exploitation in Europe's largest economy despite promise of free training
picked.body: In late August, Hong Hanh, 23, attended a conciliation hearing with her former employer at the Berlin Chamber of Commerce and Industry (IHK Berlin) to contest what she says was an unlawful dismissal. The Ho Chi Minh City native had spent nine months in Germany, shocked by her meager take-home pay and constant work. When exhaustion forced her to ask for sick leave, she said, her broker and the restaurant owner pressed her to sign a voluntary resignation that would strip her of unemployment benefits. She refused and was immediately handed a dismissal notice. The restaurant owner did not attend the hearing, sending a lawyer who argued the dismissal was valid because Hanh had shown no interest in the job. With no agreement reached, her industry's trade union is providing legal support to take the case to the Labor Court, which is expected to hear it late this year. "When I came to Germany for vocational training, I could not have imagined going through these difficulties," Hanh said. Germany is Europe's largest economy and the world's third largest, behind the U.S. and China, according to International Monetary Fund data. Vocational training in Germany took off among Vietnamese around 2018-2019 as the country eased its rules, including through the Skilled Immigration Act, to address labor shortages. The biggest draw is the dual "Ausbildung" model, under which trainees pay no tuition and receive a monthly training wage. Some Vietnamese brokers went on to market it as a route to a better life. About 16,000 young Vietnamese are now in vocational training in Germany, according to the Federal Employment Agency. Germany's Migration Report 2024 says Vietnamese made up 21% of foreign nationals who entered the country for vocational training. Income shock Hanh learned of the route from a friend while in her second year of university and dropped out to study German. In late 2025, after paying €7,000 (US$7,900) in broker fees, she arrived in Berlin. She worked at a local restaurant while waiting for her course to formally begin, and realized the high income the broker had advertised blurred gross pay (Brutto) with take-home pay (Netto). Her contract set gross pay at €1,068 a month, but she took home only €787, half of which went on rent. Although her payslip listed a "meal allowance," she still paid €68 a month out of pocket to eat at work. "I have to budget every cent of the little that is left," she said. To survive in a city as expensive as Berlin, many trainees in her position share rooms without a formal rental contract. With no name on a mailbox, they miss important letters from the authorities and insurers. Short of money, some work off the books in restaurants for less than the minimum wage, with no contract and no days off. They know they are being exploited but put up with it because of living costs and debts back home. Under German rules, recruitment fees are paid by the hiring employer. But a study published in August 2025 by the Berlin-based Minor institute found that 57% of Vietnamese trainees came to Germany through private brokers, paying fees of €6,000-15,000 ($6,750-16,900). A 2024 study by Freie Universität Berlin and reports by public broadcaster ARD estimated the figure could reach €20,000-40,000 ($22,500-45,000). Many families who spend tens of thousands of euros believe their children are securing a stable future in Europe. At an elderly care provider in Altenburg, in the state of Thuringia, a scandal broke in early 2026. The provider had lost its training license in August 2025 but concealed the fact, making 27 Vietnamese nursing trainees work unpaid for four to eight months while living in containers. In mid-January 2026, when the trainees went on strike to demand their rights, they were evicted from their accommodation in the snow. "By the time they called for help, they had lost everything: housing, their training place, their jobs and their income," Michael Tirp, director of VDP Personal Bildung Integration, which runs an emergency SOS hotline for Vietnamese workers in Germany, told VnExpress . The organization immediately launched a fundraising drive to arrange temporary housing for the group. Phuong Nga, 24, from the outskirts of Hanoi, was among them. Unpaid for half a year and left without a training place, she sheltered at a nail salon on money sent by her family. Tirp said that within a month the organization had helped her sign a contract with a new employer and find her own apartment. Hanh also described being exploited. German labor law requires a break of at least 30 minutes on shifts of six to nine hours, but she said the restaurant's timekeeping system always showed her working eight hours with a break and erased all overtime records. Worn out, she fell ill and was fired. "The broker told me to just sign the resignation and they would find me another place. When I refused because my family was already financially drained, he threatened that he had other ways to collect money from me

picked.t: Hong Kong police arrest 127 in Vietnamese-led loan sharking syndicate
picked.body: The arrests, made on Oct. 8 and 9, followed a six-month undercover operation targeting the group, which allegedly operated in West Kowloon. The syndicate was also suspected of running illegal rotating savings schemes and helping illegal immigrants obtain forged identity documents and construction worker cards. Those arrested comprised 55 men and 72 women aged between 23 and 92. Thirty-seven were Vietnamese nationals. Police said most of the syndicate's key members were Vietnamese people holding Hong Kong identity cards. Ten suspects were identified as core members, including the alleged ringleader, a Vietnamese woman who holds a Hong Kong identity card, the South China Morning Post reported. "The group’s operations were very closed, recruiting only among its compatriots," Superintendent Chiew Tsi-huen of the Organized Crime and Triad Bureau said on Saturday. Police believe the syndicate had been operating for at least a year, using grocery stores and a Vietnamese association as fronts. The group allegedly provided temporary accommodation and forged Hong Kong identity cards or construction worker cards for illegal immigrants, charging HK$2,000 to HK$2,500 (US$254 to US$318) per document to help them secure jobs, The Standard reported. The syndicate was also suspected of operating several illegal gambling venues offering baccarat and card games, as well as two bars without liquor licenses. Police believe drugs were supplied at these locations. Loan sharking and illegal savings schemes Lending was the syndicate's main source of income. Borrowers were reportedly charged HK$100 in daily interest on a HK$10,000 loan. Police said the effective annual interest rate could far exceed Hong Kong's legal cap of 48%, according to the South China Morning Post . The group also allegedly drew borrowers into illegal rotating savings schemes known locally as hui . Each scheme involved 20 members contributing HK$5,000 over 10 days to build a common fund of HK$100,000. The suspected female ringleader controlled the distribution of the money, while participants faced additional fees and were not given clear information about how the funds were allocated. Borrowers unable to repay their debts were allegedly threatened, assaulted or unlawfully detained. Some were reportedly forced to participate in drug trafficking. Police said the syndicate was divided into separate units responsible for promoting loans, collecting debts and carrying out acts of violence. The group targeted Hong Kong's Vietnamese community, a focus that police believe complicated the investigation. Many debtors were reportedly reluctant to report suspected crimes because of language barriers or concerns about their immigration status, The Standard reported. During searches, police seized more than HK$2 million in cash and valuables, along with loan records, document-forging equipment, gambling devices and drugs. Officers also seized a car worth about HK$400,000 at the suspected ringleader's home. All 127 suspects remain in custody as police investigate their backgrounds, sources of funds and alleged roles in the syndicate. Further arrests have not been ruled out.

picked.t: Southeast Asian capital sees travel interest spike for Eurovision Asia Grand Final
picked.body: Vietnam recorded the region's strongest growth, with travel interest surging 105% from 2025, according to online travel platform Agoda. India ranked second with a 43% increase, highlighting continued demand among Indian travelers for short-haul trips to Southeast Asia. Malaysia saw a more modest 4% rise, building on its established travel ties with Thailand. The contest marks a milestone for the region: the first-ever pan-Asian expansion of the 70-year-old Eurovision franchise, bringing finalists from 11 countries to the stage for a potential regional audience of millions. Visitors heading to Bangkok for the Grand Final can choose from four neighborhoods, each offering a different experience. Siam is ideal for shopping and easy transport connections, with major malls, boutiques and cultural attractions. Thonglor and Ekkamai cater to nightlife lovers with cocktail bars, live music venues and popular restaurants, Agoda recommended. Sathorn offers upscale hotels, fine dining and rooftop bars with skyline and river views. For a taste of Thai heritage, Bangkok's Old Town features landmarks such as the Grand Palace, Wat Pho and Wat Arun, alongside traditional canals and historic streets. Thailand's capital Bangkok has been named the world's best city in this year's Readers' Choice Awards by British travel magazine Condé Nast Traveller.
